title: The Fugitive's Theatre: from the House of the Red and White Lions to the Green Hill
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House of the Red and White Lions

stops.name: Leipzig, the Bruhl: the ninth child
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the house called the Red and White Lions, at No. 3 the Bruhl in the Jewish quarter of Leipzig, a ninth child is born to the police clerk Carl Friedrich Wagner and his wife Johanna Rosine. They name him Wilhelm Richard. Six months later the father is dead of typhus, in the war year that ends with Napoleon losing the Battle of the Nations at the city gates. The boy will remember none of it. He will spend his working life composing about inheritances that arrive with a curse attached and fathers who are not where the son needs them to be.
suggested_refs: Haus zum Roten und Weissen Loewen, Bruehl 3, Leipzig, demolished; site marked in the modern city
sources: Ernest Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

stops.name: Dresden, the actor Geyer takes the household
stops.date_confidence: attested: the marriage, 28 August 1814; the research pool folded it into a single wrong date with the father's death of November 1813
stops.campa: Johanna marries Ludwig Geyer, actor, painter and singer, and the household moves to Dresden where Geyer holds an engagement. Geyer teaches the boy to draw, puts him on stage as a child extra, and leaves him a name he will dispute for the rest of his life: he is enrolled at school as Richard Geyer and suspects, without ever settling it, that his stepfather was his father. Geyer dies in September 1821, seven years into the arrangement. The suspicion outlives him and walks into the operas as a question about who fathered whom.
suggested_refs: Ludwig Geyer's portraits and stage roles at the Dresden court theatre, 1814-1821
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

stops.name: Dresden, the Kreuzschule at the Kreuzkirche
stops.date_confidence: attested: 2 December 1822, not the 1821 given in summary chronologies
stops.campa: Before Geyer's death the seven-year-old is already boarding at Pastor Wetzel's village school at Possendorf, south of Dresden; on 2 December 1822 he enters the Kreuzschule beside the Kreuzkirche, still under the name Geyer. He takes Greek willingly and the rest under protest, and decides that what he wants to make is tragedy. A performance of Weber's Der Freischuetz reaches him in these years and does the rest. The school turns out a boy who reads the Greek dramatists for pleasure and has had no systematic music lesson of any kind.
suggested_refs: The Dresden Kreuzschule register, entry of 2 December 1822

stops.name: Leipzig, the Nikolaischule and Leubald
stops.date_confidence: month attested (January 1828); day defaulted
stops.campa: Back in Leipzig at the Nikolaischule by the Nikolaikirche, he writes Leubald, a tragedy soaked in Shakespeare in which the dead do not stay dead. He intends to set it to music, which requires knowing how, so he teaches himself composition from a borrowed treatise and works at it in secret against the wishes of a family that wants a scholar out of him. He is fifteen. The decision he makes here he never revises: the words and the music are one job, done by one man, or they are not worth doing.
suggested_refs: The manuscript of Leubald, Wagner's first completed dramatic work
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

stops.name: Leipzig University, Weinlig and the woman on the stage
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the enrolment; day defaulted. The Schroeder-Devrient performance belongs to 1829
stops.campa: In 1829 he watches Wilhelmine Schroeder-Devrient on the Leipzig stage and dates his whole artistic vision afterwards to that evening, a dramatic soprano who inhabits a role instead of delivering it. In 1831 he enrols at Leipzig University and is taken as a private pupil by Christian Theodor Weinlig, Thomaskantor, who holds Bach's old post at the Thomaskirche. Weinlig gives him six months of strict counterpoint and then tells him there is nothing further to teach. It is the only formal training Wagner ever completes.
suggested_refs: Weinlig's counterpoint exercises with Wagner, Leipzig 1831-1832
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

segments.name: The Provincial Theatres and the Sea

stops.name: Wuerzburg, the bottom rung of the trade
stops.date_confidence: season attested (1833/34); day defaulted
stops.campa: His brother Albert, a singer at the Wuerzburg theatre, gets him the post of chorus coach and director of pantomime for the 1833/34 season. He drills singers, arranges other men's operas, and works at his own first full opera, Die Feen, after a Gozzi fable; the full score is finished in January 1834 and is not staged in his lifetime. He is twenty. He has learned the thing no conservatory teaches, which is how a theatre actually runs from the inside, and how little money passes through it.
suggested_refs: The converted Anna convent at Theaterstrasse 18, Wuerzburg, the house of the 1833/34 season
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

stops.name: Koenigsberg, the Tragheim church
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At Magdeburg he is musical director of a company permanently short of money; Das Liebesverbot goes up in 1836 and closes before the second performance when the troupe collapses in debt. He follows the actress Minna Planer to Koenigsberg, where a theatre has taken her on, and marries her at the Tragheim church on 24 November. The Koenigsberg house fails in its turn. The pattern of the next thirty years is fixed here and does not vary: a post, a production, a creditor, a departure by night.
suggested_refs: The Tragheim church, Koenigsberg, destroyed 1944-1945; site in present-day Kaliningrad
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

stops.name: Riga, the German theatre and the seized passport
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed from the start of the 1837 season
stops.campa: Riga engages him as music director of its German theatre, and for two seasons he conducts a heavy repertory of other men's work in a Baltic city under Russian rule. He begins Rienzi here, on a scale no German house of the day can mount. A rival maneuvers against him and his contract is not renewed; the debts of Magdeburg and Koenigsberg have followed him and multiplied. The Russian authorities hold his passport. There is no road out of the empire with an inspector on it that he can use.
suggested_refs: The Rigaer Stadttheater, Wagner's podium 1837-1839, later the Latvian National Opera
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

stops.name: Pillau, boarding the Thetis
stops.date_confidence: month attested (July 1839); day reconstructed
stops.campa: Wagner and Minna cross the Russian border in secret, without passports, and board the merchant ship Thetis at the port of Pillau, bound for London. The sea is chosen because the land is watched. The crossing is planned for eight days and takes three and a half weeks. He is twenty-six, with a bankrupt theatre behind him, no engagement ahead of him, and the unfinished score of Rienzi in the luggage of a man who has just committed the first of his professional disappearances.
suggested_refs: The harbour of Pillau, now Baltiysk, point of embarkation July 1839
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

stops.name: The Norwegian coast, the sailors' shout
stops.date_confidence: month only; the inlet itself is disputed by biographers
stops.campa: A storm drives the Thetis off course and the crew puts in among the rocks of the Norwegian coast to shelter. Wagner tells it afterwards as the founding event of Der fliegende Hollaender: the sailors' shout coming back off the granite in a hard echo, the seamen's legend of the damned captain retold in the forecastle, the sound world of the opera arriving whole. He set the story down decades later, from memory, in an autobiography written for a king. Biographers dispute the inlet and the arrangement of the memory alike.
suggested_refs: Sandviken and the Norwegian inlets proposed as the Thetis anchorage, none confirmed
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

segments.name: Paris Hunger and the Dresden Kapellmeister

stops.name: Paris, the Rue de la Tonnellerie lodgings
stops.date_confidence: arrival in Paris attested to September 1839; exact day reconstructed
stops.campa: Landing at Boulogne, he seeks out Giacomo Meyerbeer, the most powerful opera composer in Europe, who is summering there and receives him kindly and writes letters that open no doors. A week in London lies between the ship and the coast road. In Paris he takes lodgings off the Rue de la Tonnellerie and spends nearly three years doing hack arrangements for the publisher Schlesinger, setting other men's tunes for cornet and for voice with guitar. Rienzi and Der fliegende Hollaender are finished in these rooms. The Opera will not have him.
suggested_refs: Wagner's Paris hack work for Maurice Schlesinger, 1840-1842
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

stops.name: Dresden, Rienzi and the court post
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Rienzi opens at the Koenigliches Hoftheater on 20 October 1842 and plays late into the night to an audience that will not go home. Der fliegende Hollaender follows on the same stage on 2 January, and within months he is Royal Saxon Court Kapellmeister with a salary, a uniform and a pension in view: the only secure employment of his life. He is twenty-nine. He conducts Beethoven's Ninth, writes memoranda on the reform of the Saxon theatre that his employers file unread, and finds the security intolerable inside two years.
suggested_refs: The Koenigliches Hoftheater, Dresden, burnt 1869; the Semperoper stands on the site
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 1

stops.name: Dresden, Tannhaeuser and the Bohemian hills
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He drafts the Tannhaeuser prose scenario at the Bohemian spa of Teplitz in the summer of 1842, walking in the hills above the town, and the opera reaches the Dresden stage on 19 October 1845. The court finds it long and strange. He is already at the Norse and Germanic sources, already sketching Lohengrin, already writing what the court reads as sedition about how theatres should be run and who should pay for them. The Kapellmeister of the Royal Court is turning into something the Royal Court has no use for.
suggested_refs: Teplice (Teplitz), Bohemia, where the 1842 Tannhaeuser prose draft was written

stops.name: Dresden, the barricades at the Kreuzkirche
stops.date_confidence: attested: rising from 3 May, flight 9 May, warrant 16 May 1849
stops.campa: In May the barricades go up in Dresden and Wagner is inside them. He orders hand grenades from a brass founder, keeps watch from the tower of the Kreuzkirche and sends down word of the Prussian troop movements, and stands with Mikhail Bakunin, the Russian anarchist who has been sleeping under his roof. On the ninth the rising is crushed and he leaves the city. A warrant is posted on the sixteenth naming him politically dangerous. The Royal Saxon Court Kapellmeister now has a description in the police gazette.
stops.quote: suddenly became conscious of the cry raised on all sides: 'To the barricades! to the barricades!' Driven by a mechanical impulse I followed the stream of people, which moved once more in the direction of the Town Hall in the Old Market-place.
stops.quote_source: Richard Wagner, My Life (Mein Leben), vol. 1, Gutenberg ebook 5197, on the May 1849 Dresden uprising
suggested_refs: The Dresden arrest warrant of 16 May 1849 and its printed description of Wagner
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 2

stops.name: Magdala, the borrowed passport
stops.date_confidence: mid-May 1849; the exact days of the concealment are not fixed in the reachable sources
stops.campa: He reaches Weimar, where Liszt is rehearsing his Tannhaeuser, and is hidden out in the Thuringian countryside at Magdala while the Saxon police work outward from Dresden. He crosses into Switzerland on a passport belonging to Professor Widmann of Jena, obtained through Jena contacts; the popular version, in which Liszt shelters him at the Altenburg and forges the document himself, is not what the record says. He does not set foot in a German state again for twelve years.
stops.quote: the composer of an opera which was being performed there on that very day had been obliged to leave Weimar suddenly because the warrant for his arrest had arrived from Dresden.
stops.quote_source: Richard Wagner, My Life, vol. 1, Gutenberg ebook 5197, reporting village gossip about himself while in hiding
suggested_refs: The Widmann passport of Jena, on which Wagner crossed into Switzerland
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 2

stops.name: Zurich, the Hotel Zum Schwert and the artwork of the future
stops.date_confidence: arrival late May 1849; the essay published in November, day defaulted
stops.campa: He takes a room at the inn Zum Schwert, a stateless man of thirty-six with no theatre, no income and no country that will have him. Minna follows. Cut off from every stage that might perform him, he writes instead. The Artwork of the Future appears within months, arguing that opera as practised is a corruption and that the separated arts must be fused again into one work, the Gesamtkunstwerk, on the model he believes the Greeks had. The theory of the total artwork is composed by a man who cannot get a bar of music played.
stops.quote: Possible revenues from the opera I shall write for Paris I might then entirely devote to the payment of the debts I left in Dresden.
stops.quote_source: Wagner to Franz Liszt, Letter 19, Correspondence of Wagner and Liszt, vol. 1, trans. Francis Hueffer, Gutenberg ebook 3835
suggested_refs: Das Kunstwerk der Zukunft (The Artwork of the Future), Leipzig 1849
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 2

stops.name: Weimar, Lohengrin without its composer
stops.date_confidence: month attested (August 1850); the 28th is the traditional date, Goethe's birthday
stops.campa: Liszt conducts the premiere of Lohengrin at Weimar in the town Goethe made, while the composer sits four hundred miles away under a warrant and cannot come. He follows the performance by the clock, holding a watch in Zurich to know which scene is passing. He will not hear the opera himself for eleven years. Liszt keeps the work on the one German stage willing to take a political risk with it, and from now on Wagner's German reputation is built for him, in his absence, by other men's orchestras.
suggested_refs: Liszt's Weimar Hoftheater seasons and the Altenburg, his residence above the town
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 2

stops.name: Zurich, Judaism in Music
stops.date_confidence: September 1850 attested for the first printing; the exact issue date is not fixed here
stops.campa: The Neue Zeitschrift fuer Musik at Leipzig prints Das Judenthum in der Musik under the pseudonym K. Freigedank, free thought. The essay argues that Jews are incapable of art, and it names Meyerbeer, who fed him in Paris, and Mendelssohn, lately dead. He reissues it in 1869 under his own name and enlarged. The tract is not an aside beside the work; it is published in the same years and by the same hand as the books that construct the Gesamtkunstwerk, and it has never since been read apart from them.
suggested_refs: Das Judenthum in der Musik, Neue Zeitschrift fuer Musik, September 1850; expanded edition 1869

stops.name: Zurich, the four libretti of the Ring
stops.date_confidence: completion attested to 1852; the December day is reconstructed
stops.campa: Opera and Drama appears in 1851, and A Communication to My Friends beside it. By the end of 1852 the four libretti of Der Ring des Nibelungen are finished, written backwards from Siegfried's death to the theft of the gold, out of Norse and Germanic myth. No theatre in Europe can stage what he has written and no orchestra is sized for it; the singers it requires have not been trained; the machinery it calls for does not exist. He reads the text aloud to friends in Zurich rooms over four evenings and starts composing anyway.
stops.quote: I remained unshaken in my resolve to produce my Nibelungen dramas just as though the present operatic stage did not exist, since the ideal theatre of my dreams must of necessity come sooner or later.
stops.quote_source: Richard Wagner, My Life, vol. 2, Gutenberg ebook 5144
suggested_refs: The privately printed 1853 text of Der Ring des Nibelungen, twenty years before the music was done
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 2

stops.name: London, the Hanover Square Rooms
stops.date_confidence: season attested to spring 1855; the March day is reconstructed
stops.campa: The Philharmonic Society brings him over for the 1855 season. The English press treats him as a dangerous continental theorist, the orchestra gets one rehearsal to a concert, and the fee turns out thin. Queen Victoria attends one of the concerts and he is presented to her afterwards. He goes back to Zurich exhausted and no richer, to a score of Die Walkuere that no one has commissioned, in a city where nobody has asked for it, paid for by nobody in particular.
stops.quote: What I could possibly hope for from a Paris success would not even be able to keep me alive; for, without being thoroughly dishonest, I should have to hand it over to my creditors.
stops.quote_source: Wagner to Franz Liszt, Letter 27, Correspondence of Wagner and Liszt, vol. 1, trans. Francis Hueffer, Gutenberg ebook 3835, written during the Zurich exile
suggested_refs: The Hanover Square Rooms, London, home of the Philharmonic Society concerts until 1869
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 2

stops.name: Zurich, the Asyl on the Wesendonck hill
stops.date_confidence: attested: the move to the Asyl, 28 April 1857
stops.campa: Otto Wesendonck, a silk merchant enriched in New York, buys a hill above the lake at Enge and lets Wagner the cottage beside his villa for a nominal rent. Wagner names it the Asyl, the refuge. He puts the Ring down in the middle of Siegfried and begins Tristan und Isolde, having been handed Schopenhauer by the poet Georg Herwegh in 1854 and read him through again and again. Mathilde Wesendonck is his patron's wife. He writes the greatest music yet made about wanting what cannot be had, in a house her husband pays for.
suggested_refs: The Villa Wesendonck in the Rieterpark, Enge, now the Museum Rietberg; the Asyl stood beside it
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 2

stops.name: Venice, the Palazzo Giustinian in Dorsoduro
stops.date_confidence: arrival in Venice attested to late August 1858; the day is reconstructed
stops.campa: Minna intercepts a letter to Mathilde and the arrangement ends. Wagner leaves for Venice alone and takes rooms in the Palazzo Giustinian on the Grand Canal beside Ca' Foscari, where he works through the second act of Tristan with the gondoliers' calls coming up off the water. Austria rules Venice and the Saxon warrant still stands: the police let him stay, then move him on. Minna is in Dresden. The marriage has eight years left to run and is over.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Giustinian, Dorsoduro, Venice, Wagner's rooms 1858-1859
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 2

stops.name: Paris, the Jockey Club at the Salle Le Peletier
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Napoleon III orders Tannhaeuser staged at the Opera and Wagner spends months on a French version, refusing to move the ballet into the second act where the Jockey Club members arrive after dinner. They come to the first night with whistles. Three performances are shouted down and he withdraws the production himself. Charles Baudelaire, who had already written him a letter of recognition out of nowhere, publishes a defence within weeks. The failure makes him famous in France, which the success would not have done.
suggested_refs: Baudelaire, Richard Wagner et Tannhaeuser a Paris (1861)
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 3

stops.name: Vienna, the seventy rehearsals at the Kaerntnertortheater
stops.date_confidence: the abandoned production runs 1862-1864; day defaulted
stops.campa: The Vienna Court Opera takes Tristan und Isolde for the Kaerntnertortheater and rehearses it more than seventy times across two years before abandoning it as unperformable. The tenor breaks down. Wagner, in the city and then hiding inside it, borrows against fees he has not earned for operas nobody has staged. By the spring of 1864 the creditors are near enough that he leaves at night. He is fifty years old, the Ring is half composed, and Tristan exists as ink and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The Kaerntnertortheater, Vienna, demolished 1870; site by the modern Opernring
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 3

stops.name: Biebrich, the villa on the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is reconstructed from the amnesty of 1862
stops.campa: The Saxon amnesty lets him back into Germany and he rents rooms in a villa at Biebrich on the Rhine, near Wiesbaden. Here he begins composing Die Meistersinger von Nuernberg, a comedy about a singing contest and the rules of art, written by a man who has spent thirteen years in print arguing that the rules are wrong. Minna comes from Dresden to see him. They quarrel for ten days and she goes. It is the last time husband and wife meet; she has four years left. He is bankrupt again by the autumn.
suggested_refs: The Biebrich villa on the Rhine, where the Meistersinger composition began
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 3

stops.name: Munich, the Residenz: the king's messenger
stops.date_confidence: attested: Stuttgart 3 May, the Munich audience 4 May 1864. The research pool's 'March 1864' for Stuttgart is wrong
stops.campa: He goes to ground in Stuttgart on the third of May under an assumed name, ahead of the Vienna warrants, and the next morning a stranger sends up a card: Franz von Pfistermeister, cabinet secretary to Ludwig II of Bavaria, eighteen years old and weeks on the throne, who has been hunting for the author of the Ring poem across Germany. On the fourth Wagner is received at the Residenz in Munich. Within days the king has paid the debts, settled a stipend and a house on him, and asked what he needs to finish the cycle.
stops.quote: In words which, though few, penetrated to the very core of my being, the youthful monarch confessed his great partiality for my work, and announced his firm resolve to keep me near him as his friend, so that I might escape any malignant stroke of fate.
stops.quote_source: Richard Wagner, My Life, vol. 2, Gutenberg ebook 5144, on Ludwig II's first message, delivered by Pfistermeister at Stuttgart, 3-4 May 1864
suggested_refs: The Munich Residenz, audience chamber of Ludwig II, 4 May 1864
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 3

stops.name: Munich, Tristan und Isolde reaches a stage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Tristan und Isolde is given at the Koenigliches Hof- und Nationaltheater under Hans von Buelow, whose wife Cosima is already carrying Wagner's first child. Vienna judged the work impossible; Munich plays it four times. Ludwig sits in his box and writes to Wagner afterwards in the language of a man converted rather than entertained. By December the Bavarian cabinet and the Munich press have made the composer's presence a constitutional nuisance, and the king who summoned him is compelled to send him away.
suggested_refs: The Koenigliches Hof- und Nationaltheater, Munich, site of the Tristan and Meistersinger premieres
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 3

stops.name: Tribschen, the house on the lake
stops.date_confidence: attested: the lease runs 30 March 1866 to 22 April 1872
stops.campa: He leases Tribschen, a house on a promontory over Lake Lucerne, and holds it six years. Minna dies in Dresden that January and he does not go to the funeral. Cosima von Buelow comes and does not go back: Liszt's daughter, Buelow's wife, twenty-four years younger than Wagner and already the mother of two of his daughters, both born in Munich. Their son Siegfried is born in this house in 1869. Ludwig pays for the arrangement. Buelow goes on conducting the operas of the man his wife is living with.
suggested_refs: Villa Tribschen, Lucerne, now the Richard Wagner Museum of the city
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 4

stops.name: Munich, Die Meistersinger von Nuernberg
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The comedy is given in Munich under Buelow with the king in the royal box and Wagner beside him, which the court reads as a provocation and the public as a triumph. It ends with the cobbler Hans Sachs warning his townsmen to honour their German masters and hold the holy German art safe. The wars that will make a German empire are running while the score is written. Nuremberg will be remembered for that last scene in ways its composer cannot arrange and does not live to see.
suggested_refs: The closing address of Hans Sachs, Die Meistersinger, act three
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 4

stops.name: Leipzig, the Brockhaus parlour: Nietzsche
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the Leipzig house of the Brockhaus family, into which Wagner's sister had married, a philology student of twenty-four is brought to meet him. Friedrich Nietzsche has known Tristan from the piano score for years. Wagner plays passages from the unfinished Meistersinger, talks Schopenhauer, and mimics the Leipzig professors; Nietzsche leaves electrified and writes about it the same night. Wagner is fifty-five, the age of Nietzsche's dead father. The friendship lasts ten years and the argument with it lasts the rest of Nietzsche's working mind.
suggested_refs: Nietzsche's letters of November 1868 describing the first meeting

stops.name: Lucerne, the Protestant church
stops.date_confidence: attested; the divorce was granted by a Berlin court on 18 July 1870, not in Munich as the research pool has it
stops.campa: Cosima's divorce from Hans von Buelow is finalised by a Berlin court in July, and on the twenty-fifth of August she and Wagner marry in the Protestant church at Lucerne, not in the Catholic Hofkirche that some accounts name. She is thirty-two and he is fifty-seven. From this year she keeps the diaries: fourteen years of daily entries addressed to their children, recording what he says at table, what he dreams, what he thinks of Jews and of Bismarck. They become the largest source for his life and the most interested one.
suggested_refs: The Matthaeuskirche, Lucerne, the Protestant church of the 1870 marriage

stops.name: Tribschen, the Siegfried Idyll on the stairs
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On Christmas morning, the birthday Cosima keeps, fifteen musicians assemble on the stairs at Tribschen and play a piece she has never heard, written in secret out of the themes of Siegfried and a cradle song. She wakes to it coming up the staircase. Nietzsche is one of the household's regulars in these years, twenty-three visits between 1869 and 1872, and calls Tribschen the one true home of his adult life. The house works as an island: no theatre, no orchestra, no public, and the Ring moving forward at last.
suggested_refs: The Siegfried Idyll, first performed on the Tribschen staircase, 25 December 1870

stops.name: Bayreuth, the foundation stone in the rain
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The town council of Bayreuth, a Franconian town with a baroque opera house too small for him and no musical politics of its own, grants land on a hill north of the streets. On his fifty-ninth birthday, in rain, Wagner lays the foundation stone of a theatre that does not yet have its money, and conducts Beethoven's Ninth that afternoon in the old margravial house. Nietzsche is in the audience. The building will be paid for by subscription, by patronage societies, and in the end by the king who has already paid for everything else.
suggested_refs: The margravial opera house, Bayreuth, where the Ninth was conducted on 22 May 1872
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 4

stops.name: Bayreuth, Wahnfried and the grave in the garden
stops.date_confidence: attested: 28 April 1874. The '18 April' circulating in summary chronologies is a transcription error
stops.campa: The family moves into the house he has built at the edge of the Hofgarten and named Wahnfried, here where my delusions found peace, and the words are cut into the front of it. Ludwig's loan paid for the building. Behind the house, in the garden, the vault is dug and finished before the family is properly moved in: Wagner has chosen the ground he means to be buried in and shows it to visitors. He is sixty-one. Goetterdaemmerung is finished that November and one opera remains.
suggested_refs: Haus Wahnfried, Bayreuth, with the inscription over the door and the vault behind
sources: Newman, The Life of Richard Wagner, vol. 4

stops.name: Bayreuth, the Festspielhaus opens with the Ring
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Festspielhaus opens with Das Rheingold: an auditorium with no boxes and no centre aisle, raked like a Greek amphitheatre, dark through the performance, and the orchestra sunk out of sight beneath a hood so the sound arrives with no visible source. The complete Ring is given three times that August under Hans Richter, the first time the four dramas have been played in sequence anywhere. Twenty-eight years have passed since the first libretto. The festival closes with a deficit, and Ludwig II, who paid, has ten years to live.
suggested_refs: The Bayreuth Festspielhaus, sunken pit and darkened house, opened 13 August 1876

stops.name: Naples, the Villa Angri and Klingsor's garden
stops.date_confidence: the winter stay is attested to 1880; the January day is reconstructed. The Ravello visit is dated 26 May 1880 in Cosima's diary
stops.campa: His heart is failing and the doctors send him south. The family winters at the Villa Angri on the Posillipo ridge above the Bay of Naples, where he works at Parsifal and looks at the sea. On the twenty-sixth of May he walks into the overgrown garden of the Villa Rufolo at Ravello, on the cliff above Amalfi, and says that Klingsor's magic garden is found and need not be invented. Gabriele d'Annunzio will be handed Wagner in these same Naples salons a decade later, during his own years of splendid misery.
suggested_refs: Villa Rufolo, Ravello, and Cosima's diary entry of 26 May 1880

stops.name: Palermo, the last bar of Parsifal
stops.date_confidence: attested by Cosima's diary entry of 13 January 1882
stops.campa: The family moves on to Sicily for the winter, and in a room at the Hotel des Palmes in Palermo Wagner writes the last bar of the full score of Parsifal. The subject has been in his hands since the 1850s: a Grail brotherhood, a wound that will not close, a fool made wise by pity. He is sixty-eight and has thirteen months to live. Nothing else is begun after this except an essay, and the essay is not finished.
suggested_refs: Grand Hotel et des Palmes, Palermo, where the Parsifal score was completed

stops.name: Bayreuth, Parsifal and the baton taken in the pit
stops.date_confidence: attested: 26 July 1882. The research pool's '26 May 1882' is wrong by two months
stops.campa: Parsifal opens the second Bayreuth Festival under Hermann Levi, the son of a rabbi, whom Wagner keeps in the pit against the objections of the king's advisers, of his own circle, and of everything he has published on the subject since 1850. Sixteen performances run into August. At the last of them, on the twenty-ninth, Wagner takes the baton unannounced during the third act and conducts his own final scene to the end. He has stipulated that the work is to be played here and nowhere else on earth.
suggested_refs: Hermann Levi's conductorship of the 1882 Parsifal and his correspondence with his father

stops.name: Venice, Ca' Vendramin Calergi: the desk
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The family takes the mezzanine floor of the Ca' Vendramin Calergi on the Grand Canal for the winter. On the thirteenth of February Wagner is at his desk, at work on an essay called On the Feminine in the Human, when the heart attack comes. He dies that afternoon, sixty-nine years old. The essay breaks off unfinished. Cosima will not let the body be moved for a day and a night. The palazzo now houses the municipal casino of Venice, and the rooms he died in are shown to visitors who have bought a ticket for something else.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Vendramin Calergi, Venice; the unfinished essay 'Ueber das Weibliche im Menschlichen'

stops.name: Rapallo, ten days of Zarathustra
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing: the atlas file dates the ten-day burst to 1 February 1883, before the death it is said to answer
stops.campa: On the Ligurian coast at Rapallo, in this same February, Nietzsche writes the first part of Thus Spoke Zarathustra in ten days, walking the paths toward Zoagli and Portofino while the sentences arrive faster than he can set them down. The eruption is dated to the first of the month and the grief to news out of Venice, and the two dates do not fit each other; both are left as they stand. Between the two men there has been no word for five years and there is no reconciliation on record.
suggested_refs: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, part one, Rapallo, February 1883

stops.name: Bayreuth, the unmarked mound
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A special train brings the coffin from Venice to Bayreuth and he is laid in the vault under the mound in the garden of Wahnfried, thirty paces from the desk in the hall. The stone carries no name and no dates, by his own instruction: the house and the festival are to say it for him. Cosima runs the festival for the next twenty-three years and dies in 1930 at ninety-two. Her ashes stay at Coburg for forty-seven years after a dispute over the cremation and are laid at the south side of the same mound only in 1977.
suggested_refs: The Wagner grave in the garden of Wahnfried, unmarked vault under a mound

stops.name: Turin, the last argument
stops.date_confidence: the Turin burst is attested to autumn 1888; day defaulted. The collapse follows on 3 January 1889
stops.campa: In Turin, in the last lucid months, Nietzsche writes The Case of Wagner and assembles Nietzsche contra Wagner alongside Twilight of the Idols and Ecce Homo. Five years after the funeral he is still writing about the same man, and the pamphlets are as close to love letters as to prosecutions. On the third of January 1889 he is picked up in the street and sends out signed notes, one of them to Cosima Wagner at Bayreuth, signed Dionysus. The Wagner argument is the last thing his mind does before it stops.
stops.quote: Is Wagner a man at all? Is he not rather a disease? Everything he touches he contaminates. He has made music sick.
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Case of Wagner, trans. Anthony M. Ludovici, Gutenberg ebook 25012
suggested_refs: The Case of Wagner and Nietzsche contra Wagner, Turin, 1888
sources: Nietzsche, The Case of Wagner, Gutenberg ebook 25012

stops.name: Bayreuth, Isadora Duncan in the Venusberg
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Cosima, guarding the works as scripture, invites Isadora Duncan to the 1904 festival to dance the Bacchanale in the Venusberg scene of Tannhaeuser: the first outsider's body admitted to that stage. Duncan dances bare-legged and argues with the Bayreuth ballet about what a Greek wears. In 1930 Siegfried Wagner brings Rudolf von Laban to the same theatre for the same Bacchanal, with Toscanini in the pit. The Venusberg is the door through which Bayreuth keeps letting the twentieth century in, one scene at a time.
suggested_refs: Isadora Duncan's 1904 Bayreuth engagement; Laban's 1930 Tannhaeuser Bacchanal

stops.name: Bayreuth, Wahnfried's guest from Munich
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the beginning of the association; day defaulted
stops.campa: Siegfried Wagner marries the English-born Winifred Williams, and from 1923 she receives Adolf Hitler at Wahnfried, sends him writing paper in Landsberg prison, and keeps the friendship for the rest of her life. He comes to the festival later as chancellor and the house is photographed around him. Wagner has been dead forty years and cannot be consulted about any of it. What he did write, in 1850 and again in 1869 over his own name, is quoted back approvingly by the state that adopts his theatre.
suggested_refs: Frederic Spotts, Bayreuth: A History of the Wagner Festival
sources: Frederic Spotts, Bayreuth: A History of the Wagner Festival

stops.name: Bayreuth, the firebomb and the bare stage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A firebomb comes through from the south and takes about half of Wahnfried, the great hall and its rotunda; the grave in the garden is untouched. The festival reopens in 1951 under the grandsons Wieland and Wolfgang, who clear the stage of forests, horned helmets and every naturalistic thing the regime had loved, and light bare space instead. They call it New Bayreuth. The house is restored between 1972 and 1976 and opens on 24 July 1976 as the Richard-Wagner-Museum, with the desk in it and the death mask.
suggested_refs: Wieland and Wolfgang Wagner's New Bayreuth stagings from 1951; the Richard-Wagner-Museum, opened 1976
sources: Frederic Spotts, Bayreuth: A History of the Wagner Festival
